newsitem.title: UK: Moody's says EMU to spur demand for regional debt.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says EMU to spur demand for regional debt.

text.p: Moody's Investors Services said on Wednesday that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would probably spur significant investor demand for debt from European cities, regions and states.

In its first report on European "territorial community" finance (covering states in federal nations, regions, provinces, cities) Moody's said the outlook for the end of this century is for "a sharp surge in the market presence of a fast-widening number of territorial communities, from Western, Central, and Eastern Europe -- including countries of the former Soviet Union."
"The basic ingredients of such a development are already in place," Moody's said in a statement.

It cited as a reason for this the structural disparities between the growing responsibilities of European communities and the less generous resource-allocation schemes set up by central governments in the ongoing decentralisation process.

The report said political, economic, and financial decentralisations was likely to continue both in the European Union -- where the need to comply with the three percent Maastricht treaty criterion forces governments to reduce budget deficits -- and in the countries of Central and Eastern Europe.

In the latter areas, Moody's believes that the national governments view local financing as the only viable avenue for local infrastructure projects, and where the post-communist civil societies increasingly value the virtues of local self-government.

The report said the structural gap between growing powers, on the one hand, and more limited operation resources, on the other hand, is building up pressure for Europe's regions and cities to fund their rising investment needs with external financing.
Moody's said EMU "and its snowball effect would probably spur significantly investor demand for pan-European territorial-community debt".

As cross-border currency-risk and interest-rate risk would disappear as concerns for investors within the Union, and would largely diminish for investors outside the Union, credit risk would be largely left as a key parameter.
In this context, the report said that "investor interest for creditworthy territorial-community debt would clearly be keen."

On the other hand, Moody's report added that EMU would largely eliminate such idiosyncrasies as borrowing only in local currencies and in local markets (as is currently the case in Belgium and in Germany) -- thus enabling the creating of a true pan-European regional and municipal finance market.
On the use of derivatives and financial leverage, Moody's remarked that on average European communities had remained more cautious than some of their counterparts in the U.S. market.

Nevertheless, the report said that for most communities, which on average remain less financially-sophisticated, even run-of-the-mill financial leverage products such as repurchase agreements could generate losses if appropriate in-house expertise did not exist.

Furthermore, added Moody's, sometimes even if the hedging technique being used was appropriate, its ultimate cost might still exceed the potential savings the hedging was supposed to achieve to begin with.
